t: Check if Word Can Be Placed In Crossword: Slot Enumeration in Four Directions
o:
**Understanding the problem**

The grid mixes fixed letters, blank cells (' ') that accept anything, and '#' blockers. The word may run horizontally or vertically, forwards or backwards, provided no letter lands on a '#', each fixed letter it covers matches, and — crucially — the cells immediately beyond both ends of the word are '#' or the grid edge. In Example 1 the middle column forms a three-cell slot (' ', ' ', 'c'); reading bottom-up gives c-b-a, so "abc" fits vertically. In Example 2 the only open slots have length 3, and any length-2 placement would leave an open cell touching one of its ends, hence false. In Example 3 the bottom-row slot " c" accepts "ca" written right-to-left: 'c' matches and the blank absorbs 'a'. Since m*n can reach 2*10^5, the solution must stay near-linear, but verifying one placement only costs a walk along the word.
k: The boundary rule is the real constraint: nothing open may touch either end of the word, so the word must fill an entire maximal run of non-'#' cells — slots of any other length are dead ends.
Placing the word backwards equals matching a slot against the reversed word, so two string comparisons cover all four orientations.
Blank cells are wildcards; only fixed letters can cause a mismatch.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every Start Cell in Four Directions
a.i: The most direct reading of the rules: treat every cell as a potential first letter and attempt the word horizontally left/right and vertically up/down. Trying all four directions with the word as given also covers reversed placements, since laying it right-to-left from one cell equals laying it left-to-right one slot over. Each attempt walks at most len(word) cells, and the cheap boundary pre-check prunes nearly every start immediately.
s: Define blocked(x, y) as true when (x, y) lies outside the grid or holds a blocker character.
For every cell (i, j) and every direction among right, left, down, up:
Skip the start unless the cell before it, (i-dx, j-dy), is blocked — otherwise the boundary rule fails.
Walk k from 0 to len(word)-1: fail if the covered cell is blocked or holds a different fixed letter.
Require the cell just past the last letter to be blocked; if every check passes return true. Return false after all attempts.
a.t: O(m * n * L) with L = len(word) — every cell spawns four attempts of at most L steps, though boundary pre-checks prune nearly all starts at O(1) cost.
a.sp: O(1) — only direction offsets and loop indices.

a.n: Approach 2: Enumerate Maximal Slots Between Blockers
a.i: Because an open cell may not touch either end, the word always occupies a complete maximal horizontal or vertical run of non-'#' characters. So slice every row and every column at '#' characters and test each segment of matching length against both the word and its reverse. This removes redundant probing and turns the solution into almost declarative string handling.
s: Join each row into a string and split it on '#'; keep the non-empty segments.
Do the same for every column.
A segment matches when its length equals len(word) and, position by position, each fixed character agrees with the word or with the reversed word.
Return true if any collected segment matches; otherwise false.
a.t: O(m * n) — assembling and slicing every line touches each cell once, and segment checks are bounded by segment lengths.
a.sp: O(m * n) — storing the row/column strings dominates.

w:
**Takeaway**

Lead with Approach 2 in an interview: collapsing the fussy boundary rules into "the word must fill a maximal slot" reduces everything to splitting strings and doing two comparisons. Pitfalls: forgetting backwards placements (Example 3), allowing an open neighbor at a word end (Example 2), and treating ' ' as something to preserve rather than a wildcard. Likely follow-ups: place several words at once by matching slots against a dictionary (trie), or count all valid placements instead of deciding existence.
